title: The Common Feedback That You Don’t Bring People Along With You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article unpacks the vague but common feedback that a leader "doesn't bring people along," narrowing in on the communication half of that problem (as distinct from gaining buy-in through inclusion, which the newsletter says it has covered elsewhere). It describes how leaders who think several steps ahead often fail to share their reasoning before issuing directions, leaving team members confused, sometimes intentionally resistant, and prone to disengaging over time. The recommended fix is for leaders to explain what they're seeing and thinking before a plan takes shape, and then to invite the team to probe and challenge that reasoning rather than simply debating conclusions.
points: "Doesn't bring people along" often means a leader fails to share reasoning and rationale before issuing directions.
Leaders who think several steps ahead can leave teams confused or intentionally resistant when they skip explaining their logic.
Team members interpret unexplained directions as a sign of disrespect, which drives disengagement over time.
The fix is to explain thinking before a plan solidifies, then invite the team to probe and challenge the underlying reasoning.
quotes: What exactly does it mean when a leader receives the feedback that they don’t bring people along with them ?
Facile leaders and those who, like sharks, are in constant movement, often think five steps ahead of any problem, issue, or opportunity.
When the team doesn’t understand the rationale behind the leader’s directions that spring from this thinking, they don’t execute their part with rigor or vigor .
Good leaders not only take the time and make the effort to include the team with what they are thinking and seeing, they also ask them to probe their logic and evidence.
Without it, teams flounder with uncertainty and weak execution. There’s no excuse for that. Bring them along with you instead.
